text: Πληροῦσα τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐμπαθοῦς φαντασίας. Male Picus sic clara torquet, nulloque apto sensu reddit; dum non attendit ipsam participii constructionem, ac τὸ πληροῦσα, rei genitivo gaudere; quod nobis ablativo casu redditur, Libidinosa implens cogitatione.
anchorLine: ἐμπαθοῦς φαντασίας (a), ταῖς σωματικαῖς τῶν Γρα-
en: 'Filling the sense with passionate imagination.' Picus renders this badly, giving no fitting sense, since he does not attend to the participial construction itself: πληροῦσα takes a genitive, whereas we render it with an ablative, 'filling with lustful thought.' (Comment on the printed phrase; no bracketed word is involved.)

text: Καὶ ἰσχυρὸς ὁράσει. Davidem ista respiciunt, qui sic filios Saulis post ejus mortem in gratiam Gabaonitarum, grassante fame occiderit, eisque in monte crucifigendos tradiderit. Dicitur autem ἀγαθὸς ὁράσει, I Reg. xvi, 2, quod formosum, decorum aspectu, Syrus et Arab. exponunt. Hebr. ut a LXX redditum טוב Maximus qui ad animum erat, ἰσχυρὸς; fortis maluit : quasi a virtute, qua maxime animi pulchritudo consistit; potiusque active videtur accipere, ut quasi altera alteram vocem explicet, τὸ, διορατικὸς, τῷ, ἰσχυρὸς ὁράσει, fortis visu, eoque acuti : nec male Picus, risique pollens; etsi non satis ad mentem videtur sacri textus.
anchorLine: ὁράσει (b), ἀεὶ ἐφίεται καὶ ζητεῖ τὸ πρόσωπον Κυ-
en: 'And strong in sight.' These words look to David, as do those who say that he put Saul's sons to death after the king's death, in favour of the Gabaonites, in time of famine, and handed them over to be crucified on the mountain. (Elsewhere) 'good of sight' is said, 1 Kings xvi, [2 as printed], meaning 'handsome, comely in appearance,' as the Syriac and Arabic explain. The Hebrew (tov) was rendered by the Seventy; Maximus, who had the soul in mind, preferred 'strong' (ἰσχυρός), as if from virtue, in which the beauty of the soul chiefly consists; and it seems better taken actively, so that one word explains the other: 'penetrating' (διορατικός) for 'strong of sight', i.e. keen in seeing; Picus's rendering is not bad, though it hardly seems to fit the sense of the sacred text.

text: Κατασαρκούμενος ταῖς ἐναίμοις θυσίαις. Carnali sensu menteque factus cruentis hostiis ; Car-

text: [continued from p-0693 note (c), 'Κατασαρκούμενος ταῖς ἐναίμοις θυσίαις. Carnali sensu menteque factus cruentis hostiis ; Car-'] nalis inde redditus, ac velut ejus cura, et voluptas illis sanciatur, ut superioribus jam exposuit. Non bene Picus, incarnatus ruentis sacrificiis : quod ille cruentis scripserit. Quod erat, ἐν τῷ ὕψει τῆς ἀπαθείας · essetque, in imperturbationis celsitate ejusque summo axe ac vertice, allegoria ad montem, in quo crucifixi Saulis filii; non bene idem Picus, cogitationes excelsæ vacuitatis affectionum, aptius tamen quod restitui θεωρίας, exstatque quæst. illa 65, Ad Thalas.
en: [Continuing the note keyed (c) on p-0693:] '... made carnal, whence his care and pleasure are consecrated to them, as was explained above. Picus is wrong: 'incarnate by bloody sacrifices,' since the author wrote 'bloody' [or: since the Greek says 'bloody']. What stood there was 'in the height of impassibility,' so that it would be 'in the loftiness of imperturbability, at its highest peak and summit'; the allegory refers to the mountain on which Saul's sons were crucified. Again Picus is wrong ('thoughts of the lofty emptiness of passions'); though I have restored 'of contemplation' (θεωρίας) more fittingly, and that question, number 65, to Thalassius, is extant.' No bracketed word of the text is at issue.

text: Πράττειν κατὰ τὸ αὐτό. Quod sane exque philosophia optime extulit Maximus, non posse sic contraria secundum idem, id est, simul et semel, eodemque quasi munere agere, vimque exercere, quorum alterum, vitæ ; alterum, interitionis mortisque auctor exsistant ; valde ἀφιλοσόφως Picus Nequeunt circa idem agere littera et spiritus ; quæ est ipsa contrariorum essentiæ ac rationis negatio. Sunt certe illa circa idem, sed non simul, sed unum ex alio et successione.
anchorLine: δύναται καὶ τὸ γράμμα πράττειν κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ (d)
en: 'To act in the same respect.' Maximus has set this out very well from philosophy: contraries cannot act, in the same respect, that is, at once and together, in the same office, and exercise a power of which the one would be the author of life and the other of destruction and death. Picus very unphilosophically [renders]: 'Letter and spirit cannot act in the same respect' - which is the very denial of the essence and rationale of contraries. They certainly are in the same respect, but not simultaneously: one comes from the other and in succession. (No bracketed word is at issue.)

μιουργίαν ἐλλείψεως · ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς τοπικῆς [qu. 65, τυπικ.] τοῦ περιτεμνομένου μορίου θέσεως, διδασκύ-

text: Περὶ τὴν ἐπείσακτον γένεσιν. Necessario restituta vox ex mss. quæ editis deerat, et repetitur in fine capitis. Non enim circa γένεσιν absolute, sic libidinosa versatur mentis affectio, sed circa γένεσιν ἐπείσακτον, quæ ex peccato advenit naturæ, et quam Maximus non raro γέννησιν vocat, opponitque τῇ γενέσει · quæ sit simplex procreatio et ortus, qualis a Deo Adami fuit, non qui brutorum more commistione seminum ac libidine in nobis fit; quod passim Maximus post Greg Nyss. ac superiores theologos negat futurum homine non peccante. Quod τὸ, γνωμικῶς (quomodo faciendam circumcisionem spiritalem ac vere Deo acceptam monet Maximus) scite reddit. Picus, non satis scitum, est animo, voluntate, ac quod reddidi, mentis arbitrio, animique sententia.
anchorLine: περὶ τὴν ἐπείσακτον γένεσιν (e) σχέσεως, παντελὴς
en: 'Concerning the imported (ἐπείσακτον) generation.' The word has of necessity been restored from the manuscripts; it was lacking in the printed editions, and it is repeated at the end of the chapter. For the libidinous disposition of the mind is not concerned with generation absolutely, but with imported generation, which comes into nature from sin and which Maximus often calls 'begetting' (γέννησις), setting it against 'generation' (γένεσις), which is simple procreation and origin, such as Adam's from God, not the kind that in us occurs, in the manner of brutes, by the mingling of seeds and by lust; Maximus, after Gregory of Nyssa and earlier theologians, repeatedly denies that this would have happened had man not sinned. As for the word γνωμικῶς (by which Maximus teaches how the spiritual circumcision truly acceptable to God is to be performed), [Picus] rendered it cleverly; Picus, not clever enough, rendered it 'est animo, voluntate'; and what I have rendered is 'by the mind's choice and the soul's judgment.' (The editor SUPPLIES the word ἐπείσακτον from manuscripts, but it stands unbracketed in the text.)

text: Ἡ παντελὴς καθ' ὑπεροχὴν ἀγνωσία παρίστησι. Istud ex mysticæ theologiæ sinu petitum ac Dionysio, quo eminentia quædam scientiæ divinitus concessæ supra humanam denotatur ; uti et in eo quod stultum Dei nominatur, eminens quædam supra humanam sapientia ; uti Paulus I Cor. i, si-
anchorLine: παντελὴς καθ' ὑπεροχὴν ἀγνωσία παρίστησι (f).
en: 'The complete ignorance, by way of excellence, establishes.' This is taken from the heart of mystical theology and from Dionysius, in which a certain eminence of divinely granted knowledge beyond the human is denoted; as also in what is called 'the foolishness of God', a certain eminent wisdom above human wisdom; as Paul, 1 Cor. i, [signifies -- the note breaks off at 'si-'; see p-0697]. No bracketed word is at issue.

anchorLine: turæ quam Creatori ⁷⁶, ad mandati legem quod at-

text: [continued from p-0696 note (f), '... uti Paulus I Cor. i, si-'] gnificat ; explicantque theologi illa voce καθ' ὑπεροχήν, secundum excellentiam. Male Picus, prorsusque ἀμυθήτως. Ample subjicit oculis summa ignoratio.
en: [Continuing note (f) of p-0696:] '... signifies; and the theologians explain by that phrase 'καθ' ὑπεροχήν' the sense 'according to excellence.' Picus renders it badly and quite unintelligibly: 'Ample subjicit oculis summa ignoratio' ['the highest ignorance sets [it] fully before the eyes'].' No bracketed word is at issue.

text: Στέφανος χρηστότητος. Allegoria est, ejus quod psal. illo lxiv habetur, Εὐλογήσεις τὸν στέφανον τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ τῆς χρηστότητός σου, ubi χρηστότης ex parte Dei se tenet ejusque benignitatem ac clementiam sonat, qua sic annum bonis instruit, ut sit amicis quasi contexta corona : ita hic fides, tantis aucta muneribus, quanta describit Maximus. Nec satis aptum videtur quod reddit Picus, corona probitatis, quod sic nemo in eo psal. interpretatus est, ac merito ; nec enim dici potest, corona probitatis Dei, sed ejus benignitatis seu bonitatis ; non qua coronetur Dei probitas, sed qua Deus benignitate coronat ac bonitate.
anchorLine: μδ'. Στέφανός ἐστι χρηστότητος (g), πίστις κα-
en: 'Crown of kindness.' This is an allusion to what is found in Psalm lxiv: 'You will bless the crown of the year of your kindness (χρηστότης)'; there χρηστότης belongs on God's side and denotes his benignity and clemency, by which he so furnishes the year with good things that it is as it were a woven crown for his friends; so here faith is enlarged with gifts as great as Maximus describes. What Picus renders, 'crown of probity,' seems not quite apt, since no one has so interpreted that psalm, and rightly: for one cannot say 'crown of God's probity,' but [crown] of his benignity or goodness; not that God's probity is crowned, but that God crowns with benignity and goodness. No bracketed word is at issue.

ἐξ αὐτοῦ πεποιημένων μόνιμον ἵδρυσιν *.

text: Ἣν οἶδεν ὁ λόγος. Quod sic vocat Maximus, ὁ λόγος, non ipsa sacra Scriptura est, sed Dionysius, qui sic de angelis loquitur; ut quasi fundatam eorum circa Deum collocationem ac sedem significet, quæ erit et hominum beatorum, quibus Deus ipse locus futurus sit ; ex quo etiam, perennis illa ejusdem motus quies et stabilitas ; cum in tempore, quo agimus, ipso alterante, jugis sit mutatio.
anchorLine: λόγος (h) ἄμεσον εἶναι περὶ τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον, τῶν
en: 'Which the Word knows.' What Maximus here calls 'the Word' (ὁ λόγος) is not Holy Scripture itself but Dionysius, who speaks so of the angels, as if to signify their established placing and seat about God, which will also be that of the blessed among men, to whom God himself will be the place; whence also the perennial rest and stability of that same motion, whereas in time, in which we act, time itself changing, there is constant alteration. No bracketed word is at issue.

text: Τὴν κατὰ πρόθεσιν κίνησιν. Etiam quæst. illa 65, cum perspicuum sit leg. κένωσιν, seu magis χύσιν · nec Maximum aliter scripsisse. De vitæ enim carnalis sacrificio sanguinis metaphora sermo est, quem liquet non aliter quam libatione et fusione offerri. Nihil ergo ad rem, quod ita Picus reddidit, velut commotionem sanguinis, etc. Sane cohærent νέκρωσις et κένωσις, alterum in viventibus, alterum quasi in humidis et fluentibus ; κίνησις, ne vel minimum.
anchorLine: πρόθεσιν κίνησιν (i), ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν
en: 'The motion according to purpose.' Question 65 likewise, since it is clear that one should read κένωσις ('emptying') or rather χύσις ('pouring out'); and Maximus did not write otherwise. For the discourse is a metaphor of the sacrifice of the life of the flesh by blood, which, as is clear, is offered only by libation and pouring. So Picus's rendering 'as it were the commotion of blood' etc., is beside the point. Indeed νέκρωσις ('mortification') and κένωσις cohere, the one among living things, the other as among liquids and fluids; κίνησις ('motion') not in the least. (The editor gives a VARIANT/CONJECTURE: read κένωσιν or χύσιν for κίνησιν; the printed text has κίνησιν unbracketed.)

text: Πρὸς τὴν θείαν λῆξιν ὁλοκαυτουμένων. Ut Deo totæ cedant : hæc enim holocausti ratio, ut omnia Deo adoleantur, nullæque vel sacerdotis vel offerentium partes fiant ; cujusmodi Maximus nostrum hic describit sacrificium. Est enim λῆξις, μερίς, uti Suidas exponit, et quod quis sortitur eique obtingit ac illius juris exsistit. Non bene itaque Picus, ad divinam sortem consequendum : non enim adjunctum, eum sensum patitur ; etsi alias illa vox ipsum admittat ; sitque vere Deus ipse nostra λῆξις, τὸ, παῦσις, id est, hæreditas, κληρονομία, ipso Suida interprete ; dicimusque sanctos μακαρίαν λῆξιν, beatas sedes adeptos esse. Nec bene Portus illud Suid. λῆξις, παῦσις, cessatio, sedatio, exponit : melius requies, quæ ipsa æterna, nostra in Deo hæreditas est.
anchorLine: μένων (j).
en: 'Towards the divine portion of those offered as holocausts.' So that they wholly yield to God: for this is the rationale of the holocaust, that everything be burnt for God and no parts fall to priest or offerers; such is the sacrifice Maximus describes here as ours. For λῆξις is 'share' (μερίς), as Suidas explains, and what one obtains by lot and falls to him and becomes his right. So Picus, 'to attain the divine lot,' is not good, since the adjoining context does not bear that sense, though the word elsewhere admits it; and God himself truly is our λῆξις, i.e. 'inheritance' (κληρονομία), by Suidas's own interpretation; and we say that the saints have obtained a 'blessed portion', blessed abodes. Nor does Portus do well with that word of Suidas, λῆξις, 'cessation, calming': better 'rest', which is itself eternal, our inheritance in God. No bracketed word is at issue.

text: Ἐπιληπτευόμενον τοῖς ὑλικοῖς. Qui velut dæmone, sic terrenis eorumque amore teneatur, arreptitiorum more; dum hoc animus ipse patitur, quod Saul. corpore a dæmone, a quo mitius habebat, Davide pulsante citharam. Non bene Picus, Rebus materialibus, quasi morbo comitiali laboranti, quæ est altera hujus vocis acceptio, secundo loco Hesychio posita, καὶ ὁ τῇ ἱερᾷ νόσῳ συνεχόμενος · Qui sacro morbo, id est, comitiali, laborat. Sic enim laboranti non prodest mystici Davidis cithara, uti nec Sauli profuisset, si hic ejus fuisset morbus, cum auctore Traliano et experientia teste, sic correpti, nec audiant, nec videant, nec intelligant, sed omnium sensuum facultate destituti jaceant, nihil differentes a mortuis. At nec sequentia bene reddita, τὸ πονηρὸν πνεῦμα τῆς ὑλικῆς περιπετείας, Malignum spiritum temeritatis materialis. Τῆς πρὸς αἴσθησιν additum ex mss. terrenorum vicissitudo est eorumque συμπτώματα et casus, unde sic varie sensus afficitur, ac vitia nobis propignuntur : sic enim nobis hæc allegoria, πονηρὸν πνεῦμα, non materialium temeritas, quæ non tam materialium dicatur, quam intelligentium; nempe προπέτεια.
anchorLine: γνώσεως, ἐπιληπτευόμενον τοῖς ὑλικοῖς (k) τὸν ἡμέ-
en: 'Seized by epilepsy among material things.' Seized as if by a demon, so held by earthly things and by love of them, in the manner of the possessed, while the soul itself suffers this, as Saul did in body from the demon, whom he bore more mildly when David played the harp. Picus does not render well, 'Rebus materialibus, quasi morbo comitiali laboranti' ('by material things, as one suffering from the falling sickness'), which is the other meaning of the word, given second place by Hesychius, 'one held by the sacred disease,' i.e. one who suffers epilepsy. For David's mystical harp does not help one so afflicted, as it would not have helped Saul had this been his disease, as Trallian [Alexander] attests and experience bears out: those so seized neither hear nor see nor understand but lie deprived of all sensory faculty, no different from the dead. Nor are the following words well rendered: 'the evil spirit of material misfortune' (τὸ πονηρὸν πνεῦμα τῆς ὑλικῆς περιπετείας) [Picus has] 'the evil spirit of material rashness.' The words 'τῆς πρὸς αἴσθησιν' ('that toward sense-perception') the editor SUPPLIES, added from manuscripts: [the phrase means] the vicissitude of earthly things and their accidents and chances, whence the sense is variously affected and vices are engendered in us; for so for us this allegory is 'the evil spirit', not 'the rashness of material things', which is said not so much of material things as of intelligent beings, namely προπέτεια ('rashness'). (The supplied words stand unbracketed in the text.)

text: Οὐδεμία ἐμφέρεια τούτων πρὸς ἄλληλα. Picus, ut sunt illi omnia arbitraria : Nulla horum cognatio est. Effectuum scilicet et causarum. At certe novere poetæ, quorum Paulus Act. xvii, dictum refert, probatque, Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν : Ipsius et genus sumus ; ab ipso scilicet ducta cognatione, qua et Patrem vitæque auctorem ipsum habemus, imagine etiam insigniti et similitudine ; qua divinæ ipsæ dotes in nobis elucent, libertas arbitrii, et quæ huic virtutes comites sunt, præexsistuntque in Deo περισσῶς καὶ οὐσιωδῶς, ut seq. cap. Maximus ; abundanter (seu excellenter et eximie) et essentialiter ; in nobis vero, deficienter et participatione : ex quo est, ut nulla sit inter nos Deumque ἐμφέρεια : exacta scilicet similitudo, ac qualem vox illa importat ; ut sic unum alterum referat, ut quasi pro eo accipi possit ; quo spectant illa Domini verba Joan. xiv : Ὁ ἐμὲ ἑωρακὼς, ἑώρακε καὶ τὸν Πατέρα : Qui vidit me, vidit et Patrem ; cujus ἐκμαγεῖον perfectaque expressio erat, naturalis Patris naturalis Filius. Ne cui vero durior sermo videretur, quasi ἐμφέρεια sit quovis modo dicta ὁμοιότης, similitudo, quæ non omnino neganda videtur inter causas et effecta, seq. cap. velut molliens, Οὐκ ἔστιν, inquit, ἀκριβὴς ἐμφέρεια : Non est exacta repræsentatio et similitudo : ubi Pic. perinde malus interpres : Non est explorata connexio. Nugæ : ut et quod τὰς ἐνδεχομένας εἰκόνας reddit, occurrentes imagines ; pro quantas licet, vel quantas creatura referre possit ; quantæ sunt possibiles. His se fæcibus ac stercoribus impleant, quibus Græca nec aspicere libet, ut ipsam vere Patrum mentem intelligant.
anchorLine: οὐδεμία δὲ ἐμφέρεια τούτων πρὸς ἄλληλα (l), αἰτίων
en: 'No likeness (ἐμφέρεια) of these to one another.' Picus, as is his way, makes everything arbitrary: 'There is no kinship between them' -- of effects, that is, and causes. But surely the poets knew it, whose saying Paul reports and approves, Acts xvii: 'For we are also his offspring' -- kinship drawn from him, through which we have him as Father and author of life, and are marked with his image and likeness, through which the divine gifts themselves shine in us, freedom of choice and the virtues that accompany it, which pre-exist in God 'abundantly and essentially' (as Maximus says in the next chapter), 'in an eminent and exceptional way', whereas in us they exist deficiently and by participation; hence no ἐμφέρεια, that is, exact likeness of the kind that word implies, so that one would reproduce the other and could be taken for it, exists between us and God. To this look the Lord's words in John xiv, 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' [the Son being the exact impression and perfect expression of the Father, the natural Son of a natural Father]. Lest the language seem too harsh, as if ἐμφέρεια were in any way called ὁμοιότης ('likeness'), which seems not wholly deniable between causes and effects, Maximus in the next chapter, softening it, says 'There is no exact ἐμφέρεια': 'no exact representation and likeness'; here Picus is equally a bad interpreter with 'There is no explored connection.' Nonsense; so too his rendering of τὰς ἐνδεχομένας εἰκόνας as 'occurring images', for 'as many as is permitted' or 'as many as the creature can bear'; 'as many as are possible.' Let them fill themselves with these dregs and dung (at which one does not care to look in Greek), that they may truly understand the mind of the Fathers. (No bracketed word is at issue.)

anchorLine: γραφὴν δεχόμενον [ male edita δεδόμενον] · ἵν' ὅλον
en: Bracketed inline note in the Greek text: a VARIANT (the earlier printed reading, rejected). The text prints δεχόμενον ('receiving'); the bracket reports that δεδόμενον ('given') was badly printed ('male edita') in the earlier edition. Not a supply and not a deletion; the editor corrects the earlier edition to δεχόμενον.
